# Part 2 — AI Assistants {background-color="#1A1A1A"}

Providers · Models · Web, IDE, CLI · Best practice

## Before AI Assistants

::: {.goal}
The old loop was search, adapt, wait — and the waiting was the expensive part.
:::

- You searched Google for an error message and hoped someone had met it before
- You read a book chapter written for a different dataset and an older version of R
- Stack Overflow answered eventually, and sometimes told you the question was wrong
- The colleague who knew the answer was in a meeting until Thursday
- Hours passed between having a question and having a working line of code

## What an AI Assistant Actually Is

::: {.goal}
A large language model, plus an interface that lets it read your problem and write you code.
:::

- It predicts text, so it produces plausible code — plausible is not the same as correct
- It has no access to your data unless you give it access
- It answers immediately, at any hour, and never tires of the same question
- It is strongest where the task is well specified and the idiom is common
- It is weakest where your data are unusual and your intent is vague

::: {.note}
Nothing it writes becomes true because it wrote it. You still run it, and you still check it.
:::

## Three Providers That Matter

::: {.goal}
Three companies train the models that most health researchers will actually touch.
:::

| Provider | Model family | Where you meet it |
|---|---|---|
| **Google** | Gemini | Gemini app · Gemini API · Antigravity |
| **Anthropic** | Claude | claude.ai · Claude Code · Claude API |
| **OpenAI** | GPT | ChatGPT · OpenAI API |

::: {.note}
Model names turn over every few months; the three names in the middle column do not. Every model
name in the next six slides was checked against provider documentation on **16 August 2026** —
verify before you quote any of them.
:::

## Google: the Gemini Family

- **Gemini 3** is the current frontier generation; Gemini 2.5 remains the cheaper fallback
- **Gemini 3.7 Flash** heads the developer line-up, built for coding and multi-step agent work
- **Gemini 3.1 Pro** is the large-context Pro model, still labelled preview
- **Flash-Lite** tiers exist for high-volume work where cost matters more than depth
- The Gemini app is the consumer surface — files, Deep Research, Canvas, Drive

## Anthropic: the Claude Family

- Named tiers, not numbers: **Opus** the flagship, **Sonnet** the workhorse, **Haiku** the fastest
- **Claude Opus 5** is the current Opus; **Claude Sonnet 5** and **Claude Haiku 4.5** sit below it
- **Claude Fable 5** sits above Opus for the hardest long-horizon work, at a higher price
- Surfaces: claude.ai on web, desktop and mobile, plus Claude Code in the terminal
- The API documents a managed data-analyst agent: CSV in, HTML report out

## OpenAI: the GPT Family

- **GPT-5.6** is the current generation, with members named rather than numbered
- **Sol** is the frontier model, for complex professional and research work
- **Terra** balances capability against cost; **Luna** is the cheapest, for high volume
- **GPT-5.5**, the April 2026 flagship, is still available and still competent
- ChatGPT is the assistant surface; the same models are sold through the API

## What "Frontier Model" Means

::: {.goal}
Frontier means the most capable model a company has — kept closed, and rented as a service.
:::

- The weights stay with the provider; you rent access through an app or an API
- You pay per token — roughly, per word in and per word out
- New capability appears at the frontier first and reaches everything else later
- Every prompt leaves your machine, which is why confidentiality is not an optional slide
- Versions turn over in months, so record which model produced your results

## Open-Weight Models

::: {.goal}
Open weights mean you can download the model and run it on hardware you control.
:::

- **Llama 4** from Meta, released under Meta's own community licence
- **Qwen 3.5** and **Qwen 3.8** from Alibaba, and **Gemma 4** from Google — both Apache 2.0
- **DeepSeek V4** and **Mistral** (Medium 3.5, Small 3.2) fill the mid and large range
- **gpt-oss**, at 20B and 120B parameters, is OpenAI's open-weight release, Apache 2.0
- Runners such as Ollama make a good laptop or a department server enough to start

## Frontier vs Open: the Trade-Off

| | Frontier | Open-weight |
|---|---|---|
| **Cost** | Per token; no hardware to buy | Weights are free; your hardware and your time are not |
| **Privacy** | Data leaves your machine | Data can stay on the machine |
| **Control** | The model can change under you | Pin a version and keep it indefinitely |
| **Capability** | Highest available | Close behind, and the gap keeps narrowing |

::: {.note}
For identifiable patient data, the privacy row often settles the question on its own.
:::

## Health Data: the Confidentiality Question {.smaller}

::: {.goal}
Pasting a patient dataset into a chat box is a cross-border transfer of personal data, whether or
not you thought of it that way.
:::

- Consumer chat and paid API differ in retention/training defaults; figures are Anthropic's only — verify your vendor's terms
- Anthropic: content not used to train models; API data deleted within **30 days**; zero-retention is negotiated, not a checkbox
- **HIPAA-ready API access** via self-serve BAA in Console — API only, excludes Claude Code, cannot be switched off once enabled
- Malaysia's PDPA 2024 dropped the s.129 whitelist: transfers abroad need equivalent protection, breach notice, a DPO, Guidelines 03/2025
- Safe default: de-identify, or send only column names, types and a synthetic sample — you want code back, not conclusions

## Three Places to Use an Assistant

::: {.goal}
The same model behaves like three different tools depending on where you meet it.
:::

- **Web** — a browser tab; you paste in and you copy out
- **IDE** — inside the editor; it can read the project you already have open
- **CLI** — in the terminal; it can read, write and run inside your project directory
- The further along that list you go, the more the assistant can do without you
- The further along that list you go, the more carefully you must supervise it

## Web: How It Works

::: {.goal}
You bring the problem to a browser tab; the assistant never sees your project.
:::

- Describe the problem, paste a data sample, read the answer back
- Copy the generated code into your IDE and run it there
- Refine by conversation rather than by re-prompting from scratch
- Examples: the Gemini app, claude.ai, ChatGPT — all three behave the same way here
- Nothing is installed, so this is where everyone should start

## Web: Pros and Cons

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.ks}
### Strengths
- No setup at all
- Easy to compare assistants side by side
- Good for learning and one-off questions
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.ks}
### Limits
- Manual copy-paste in both directions
- The assistant cannot see your files, so you manage context by hand
:::
:::
::::

## IDE: How It Works

::: {.goal}
The assistant lives inside your editor and can see the project you already have open.
:::

- It reads the files in your workspace, so you stop pasting context by hand
- It proposes edits in place, which you accept or reject like a code review
- Example: **Positron** with **Posit Assistant**, which also sees your loaded data and plots
- Example: the **Google Antigravity** IDE, which manages several agents at once
- You still run the code, and you still read the diff before you accept it

## IDE: Pros and Cons

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.ks}
### Strengths
- It sees your data, your plots and your session
- Edits arrive as a reviewable diff
- One window for writing, running and asking
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.ks}
### Limits
- Installation, configuration and an API key
- Easy to accept a diff you did not read
:::
:::
::::

## CLI: How It Works

::: {.goal}
The assistant runs in your terminal, inside the project directory, and can act on files.
:::

- You start it in the folder; the folder is the context
- It can read files, write files, run scripts and read the errors back
- Examples: **Claude Code**, and the **Antigravity CLI** rebuilt in Go for Antigravity 2.0
- It suits multi-file, multi-step work — a whole analysis, not a single function
- Permission prompts are the safety mechanism, so do not click straight through them

## CLI: Pros and Cons

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.ks}
### Strengths
- Handles work that spans many files
- Runs the code and reads its own errors
- Fits naturally with Git and version control
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.ks}
### Limits
- The most autonomy, so the most supervision
- Least forgiving of a vague instruction
:::
:::
::::

## Google Antigravity 2.0

::: {.goal}
Google's agentic development platform, announced in its 2.0 form at I/O 2026.
:::

- Three surfaces ship together: a desktop **IDE**, a terminal **CLI**, and a Python **SDK**
- The IDE is a command centre for running several local agents in parallel
- Multi-model: Gemini by default, with Anthropic and open-weight models selectable
- Free of charge for individual developers, on macOS, Windows and Linux
- Scheduled background tasks mean an agent can work while nobody is watching it

## Web, IDE, CLI Compared

| | Web | IDE | CLI |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Setup cost** | None | Install an editor | Install and authenticate |
| **Sees your files** | No — you paste | Yes, the open workspace | Yes, the whole directory |
| **Runs your code** | No | You run it | Yes, with permission |
| **Best for** | Learning, one-off questions | Everyday analysis | Multi-file, multi-step work |

::: {.note}
Start on the web. Move to the IDE when copy-paste gets tiring. Move to the CLI when the task spans
files.
:::

## Best Practice: Plan Before You Prompt

::: {.goal}
Write the implementation plan first — the plan is the prompt.
:::

- Say what the data are, what the outcome is, and which model you intend to fit
- Give it the data dictionary: variable names, types, units, missing-value codes
- Give it reference code that already works in your group, so the output matches your house style

```r
# A plan you can hand over, stage by stage
# 1. Read    data-raw/cohort_2026.csv; "NA" and "" are missing
# 2. Explore skimr summary; check age 18-90, sbp 60-250
# 3. Assume  outcome binary; exposure = treatment; confounders = age, sex
# 4. Apply   glm(outcome ~ treatment + age + sex, family = binomial)
# 5. Assess  performance::check_model(); confusion matrix if classification
# 6. Present gtsummary table; report the estimate and 95% CI, not p alone
# 7. Publish push to GitHub; render the Quarto report; deposit the data
```

## Best Practice: Verify Everything

::: {.goal}
Generated code that runs is not the same as generated code that is right.
:::

- Run it, then check the numbers against a result you already trust
- Check the n at every step — silent row loss is the most common quiet failure
- Read every line you are about to publish; if you cannot explain it, do not ship it

```r
nrow(dat_raw)
nrow(dat_clean)                              # did a join or filter drop people?
table(dat_clean$outcome, useNA = "ifany")    # did the recode invent a category?
```

## Best Practice: Protect the Data

::: {.goal}
De-identify before you share, and know where the request actually goes.
:::

- Strip names, IC numbers, addresses, admission dates and free-text notes before sharing anything
- Prefer structure over content: column names, types, ranges and a synthetic sample
- Know your surface — consumer chat and a paid API carry different retention defaults
- Check institutional policy and your ethics approval before real data leaves the building
- If that answer is unclear, run an open-weight model locally and the question does not arise

## Best Practice: You Remain the Analyst

::: {.goal}
The assistant accelerates the analysis. It does not own it — your name is on the paper.
:::

- Vague prompts get vague code: name the variables, the model and the output you want
- Providing no resources — no data dictionary, no reference code — wastes the tool
- Planning too little costs far more time than planning would have taken
- Not verifying the output means publishing its mistakes under your name
- Letting AI be your master is the last trap; the judgement stays with you

::: {.takeaway}
REAAAPP gives the structure, the assistant gives the speed, your domain expertise gives the quality.
:::
